summary:
# LET’S EXPLORE MARS BRAIN!!!
The folds of the human brain let us think. Mars has folds too: "brain terrain", a brain-like pattern of ridges and troughs found across the Martian mid-latitudes. Its origin is still debated, but it is closely linked to near-surface ice. That makes it valuable twice over: as a record of Mars' past climate, and as a sign of the water ice future crews will need. To study it, someone has to walk there and come back safely.

Marswalk helps astronauts do that. Orbital maps cannot fully reveal the ground astronauts will encounter: hidden sand, rough surfaces and unexpected obstacles raise the energy and oxygen a walk needs, and threaten the safety of a surface mission.

Our solution follows a simple philosophy: Scout First, Then Walk. A scout rover explores the terrain around the base before astronauts set out. A published deep-learning model then maps where brain terrain is strongest in NASA HiRISE imagery, and the best areas inside the scouted ground become science targets. Marswalk then recommends a walking route that accounts for terrain difficulty, energy consumption and the resources needed for a safe return.

More than a mapping tool, Marswalk helps astronauts decide where to go, what to explore, and how far they can safely travel.

Our vision is to empower every Martian explorer to go further, make greater discoveries, and always have enough resources to return home.
details:
LET’S EXPLORE MARS BRAIN

Marswalk is an energy-aware mapping and route-planning tool designed to help astronauts safely explore Mars. Demonstrated at Arcadia Planitia, a potential Starship landing region, it addresses a critical challenge: orbital maps often fail to capture the fine terrain details that determine the actual energy and oxygen required for an EVA.

Our solution follows a Scout First, Then Walk approach:

  1. Rover Reconnaissance: A simulated rover explores within a strict energy budget, always preserving enough energy to return home. Its exploration progressively reveals high-resolution terrain. At Arcadia Planitia, it mapped 25.9% of a 3.72 km² study area across 24 exploration loops.
  2. Scientific Target Selection: A published U-Net deep-learning model (Pearson et al., 2024) identifies scientifically interesting brain terrain. The 12 highest-scoring candidate targets within the explored area are selected.
  3. Energy-Aware EVA Planning: An astronaut route is optimized using a Mars-adjusted Pandolf walking-energy model that accounts for suit mass, gravity, and terrain conditions. The route maintains a 20% energy reserve. In our demonstration, the astronaut visits five targets along a 3.66 km route, consuming 1,316 of 1,440 usable kcal. Users can change the starting point and instantly replan the route, then experience it through a first-person 3D interface with a navigation HUD.

An offline Python pipeline processes NASA datasets into terrain classifications at 2 m resolution, distinguishing firm ground, rough terrain, sand, and blocked areas. Both rover and astronaut navigation use the same least-cost pathfinding framework. The frontend is built with HTML and JavaScript and requires no backend.

Benefits

Marswalk brings reconnaissance, terrain interpretation, and route planning together in one interactive map. Users can see where the rover has explored, inspect model-highlighted brain terrain, and understand the estimated energy cost of a proposed astronaut journey.

The Arcadia demonstration makes the relationship between surface knowledge and mission planning concrete: the rover surveys only part of the study area, and the planner chooses a feasible subset of candidate locations within its energy budget. The estimates help illustrate how a mission team could weigh scientific opportunities against the effort of reaching them.

Intended impact

Our goal is to make Scout First, Then Walk a standard principle for planning future Martian Extravehicular Activities (EVAs).

We want people to go and explore Mars' brain terrain. Building on the work of Pearson et al. (2024), who showed that deep learning can find brain terrain in HiRISE images, we use computer vision as a guide for exploration: it looks across the whole landscape and points out where the brain-like folds are most developed, so that a rover's scouting and an astronaut's limited energy are spent on the places most worth visiting.

The framework can be adapted to other landing sites with HiRISE coverage, helping mission planners evaluate exploration opportunities and risks while providing students and the public with an interactive way to investigate real Martian terrain.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python 3.12, JavaScript, HTML, CSS.
  • Libraries and frameworks: NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, scikit-learn, rasterio/GDAL, pyproj, Shapely, Pillow, Matplotlib, pytest, Playwright, MapLibre GL JS, three.js, and geotiff.js.
  • NASA and scientific data: MRO HiRISE and CTX, MOLA, THEMIS, NASA JPL Mars Trek, USGS geological maps, and Perseverance mission data, including waypoints, raw images, and SuperCam chemistry.
  • Hardware: No specialized hardware required; runs in a standard web browser.
  • Development: Git, GitHub, conda, and Anthropic Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.

How it is creative

  • From the human brain to the brain of Mars: Inspired by the folds that let us think, we make Mars' own brain-like terrain the destination, with deep learning showing where to find it.
  • Progressive terrain discovery: A scratch-off map visualizes how rover reconnaissance improves terrain knowledge.
  • Unified navigation: The rover and astronaut share the same pathfinding framework, directly connecting robotic exploration with human mission planning.
  • Immersive visualization: A first-person 3D experience allows users to explore the planned EVA route beyond conventional 2D maps.

Factors our team considered

  • Safety: The rover must always retain sufficient energy to return. Astronaut routes maintain a 20% energy reserve and account for target dwell time.
  • Physical realism: The energy model incorporates Mars gravity, spacesuit mass, and terrain-dependent walking resistance.
  • Data resolution: We address the gap between approximately 20 m orbital data and meter-scale HiRISE terrain information.
  • Scientific integrity: Results are identified as measured, derived, assumed, or simulated. HiRISE is treated as reference terrain rather than ground truth. We also explicitly acknowledge that rover behavior is simulated and terrain classifications require further human validation.
  • Accessibility: A lightweight, backend-free web application with an English interface.

The full source code and data pipeline are available on GitHub: https://github.com/ssa-yu/marswalker
projectRefs: Mapping \"Brain Terrain\" Regions on Mars using Deep Learning Kyle A. Pearson, Eldar Noe, Daniel Zhao, Alphan Altinok, Alex Morgan
